analyst:
St. John’s enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 28-6 team that went 18-2 in the BIG EAST and won the league tournament, beating Providence 85-72 on March 12, Seton Hall 78-68 on March 13, and UConn 72-52 on March 14 at Madison Square Garden. The school schedule page lists the exact 28-6 overall mark and 18-2 conference record, and AP’s Selection Sunday report also identified the Red Storm as 28-6 entering the bracket. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/sports/mens-basketball/schedule))

Offensively, this is a Rick Pitino team built less on pure half-court artistry than on pressure-created possessions, second chances, paint touches, and frontcourt playmaking. In St. John’s own February game notes, during an eight-game winning streak the Johnnies were averaging 17.3 points off turnovers, while also posting 13.1 offensive rebounds and converting those into 14.8 second-chance points per game. That statistical profile shows exactly what they hunt: extra possessions first, clean late-clock execution second. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))

The clearest named offensive hub is Zuby Ejiofor. By early February, St. John’s listed Ejiofor as the team leader in scoring, rebounding, assists, and blocks at 15.7 points and 7.5 rebounds per game, which is unusual usage for a 6-foot-9 forward and points to offense flowing through him at the elbows, short roll, and low block. Against UConn on February 6, Ejiofor produced 21 points, 10 rebounds, seven assists, three blocks and two steals, while the three starting frontcourt pieces — Ejiofor, Dillon Mitchell, and Bryce Hopkins — combined for 50 points on 65.4% shooting. That game is the best single example of St. John’s preferred attack: drive pressure, interior finishing, and big-to-big connectivity rather than volume three-point dependence. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))

Specific play tendencies show up in game recaps. Against Xavier on February 9, trailing late, St. John’s extended a possession with three offensive rebounds before Oziyah Sellers’ tip-in with 16 seconds left tied the game at 78-78. In overtime, they leaned on Ejiofor for a mid-range jumper, then closed with free throws and a Sellers transition dunk. That is a concrete example of their late-game package: crash the glass, play through contact, trust Ejiofor in the middle of the floor, and finish in the paint. In the February 28 win over Villanova, the Johnnies recorded 26 assists on 32 made field goals, with Ejiofor posting a 16-point, 12-rebound, 10-assist triple-double; that game shows the counter when opponents load to the paint — St. John’s will use its frontcourt passer to trigger cuts and weak-side finishing. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2026/2/9/mens-basketball-no-17-17-st-johns-edges-xavier-87-82-in-overtime))

Defensively, the philosophy is aggressive man pressure built to force turnovers, deny rhythm, and let their length at the 3/4 spots clean up mistakes. The numbers are explicit: in the February 6 notes, opponents were averaging 13.2 turnovers per game against St. John’s, while the Johnnies owned a +4.2 turnover margin and a 15-2 record when forcing more turnovers than the opponent. They had also recorded 12 steals at Butler on January 6 and 15 steals against Bucknell on November 20. Against UConn, Silas Demary Jr. — a guard who entered top-30 nationally in assist-to-turnover ratio according to St. John’s recap — was forced into nine turnovers. Against Creighton on February 21, St. John’s held the Bluejays without a field goal for nearly nine minutes in the second half, limited them to 26.9% shooting after halftime, and forced a season-high 18 turnovers without allowing a single Creighton player to reach double figures. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))

Pitino’s coaching fingerprint is visible in documented in-game adjustments. In the 81-72 upset of No. 3 UConn on February 6, St. John’s answered an early six-point deficit with a 13-1 burst, then with the game tied at 45 in the second half forced three turnovers during a decisive 10-0 run. That is a textbook Pitino adjustment: turn the game with defensive pressure rather than schematic patience. On January 20 versus Seton Hall, St. John’s trailed by 15 with 15:40 left, then closed on a 25-7 run and won 65-60, outscoring the Pirates 33-13 over the final 15 minutes. On March 3 against Georgetown, they rallied from 48-36 down with 13:30 remaining to win 72-69 on Senior Night. Those are not abstract “comeback” labels; they are repeated examples of Pitino teams ramping pressure, changing the game’s possession count, and trusting toughness over tempo control. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-no-22-22-st-johns-takes-down-no-3-3-uconn-in-thriller-81-72))

Clutch and late-game execution is a real strength, though not always pretty. The Xavier game on February 9 is the best evidence: Sellers’ tip-in with 16 seconds left forced OT, then Sellers added a transition dunk with seven seconds left to finish an 87-82 win. Against Georgetown on March 3, Dylan Darling’s steal and layup gave St. John’s its first lead since early in the first half at 59-57 with 6:43 left, and Bryce Hopkins hit two free throws with 16.6 seconds remaining for the final margin in a 72-69 win. Against UConn on February 6, Darling drilled a go-ahead/push-ahead three with 3:13 left for a 67-62 lead, and Mitchell followed with a tip-in with 1:36 left to restore a six-point cushion in the 81-72 upset. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2026/2/9/mens-basketball-no-17-17-st-johns-edges-xavier-87-82-in-overtime))

The key players start with Ejiofor, the team’s anchor and most complete piece. He was named First Team All-BIG EAST and averaged 16.0 points on 54.6% shooting, with 25 double-digit scoring games, nine 20-point games, and a career-high-matching 33 points against Providence on January 3. His best recent stretch included 21-10-7 against UConn on February 6, 15 points in the Creighton blowout on February 21, 23 points against Georgetown on March 3, and the 16-12-10 triple-double against Villanova on February 28. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-zuby-ejiofor-bryce-hopkins-and-dillon-mitchell-garner-all-big-east-honors))

Bryce Hopkins is the secondary scorer and physical mismatch forward. In early February he was averaging 13.6 points and 5.5 rebounds; he had 13 against UConn, 15 points and 10 rebounds against Creighton, and 19 points with nine boards against Xavier. Dillon Mitchell is the glue defender/finisher: by February 6 he was at 9.4 points and 7.0 rebounds while shooting a team-best 58.6%; he added 15 points on 7-of-9 shooting against UConn and then posted 10 rebounds and a career-high seven assists without a turnover against Creighton. In the backcourt, Ian Jackson supplied perimeter scoring and disruptive defense, tying for the early team lead with 36 made threes by February 6 and then scoring 19 points with a career-high five steals against Villanova. Dylan Darling is the change-of-pace guard who has repeatedly authored winning stretches: his key late three beat back UConn and his steal/layup swung the Georgetown comeback. Oziyah Sellers is the wing finisher who has been central in close games, most notably the tying tip-in and sealing dunk versus Xavier. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))

The notable wins reveal a team that can overwhelm quality opponents physically. The 81-72 win over No. 3 UConn on February 6 showed St. John’s can beat elite competition by turning ball security into a crisis; the 81-52 demolition of Creighton on February 21 showed how destructive the defense becomes when opponents lack multiple shot creators; the 89-57 destruction of Villanova on February 28 displayed their highest-end ball movement, with 26 assists and Ejiofor’s triple-double; and the 72-52 rout of UConn in the BIG EAST title game on March 14 underscored that St. John’s entered the tournament playing its best basketball. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-no-22-22-st-johns-takes-down-no-3-3-uconn-in-thriller-81-72))

The losses are also instructive. St. John’s lost 83-82 to Iowa State on November 24, 85-74 to Auburn on November 26, 103-96 to Alabama on November 8, 78-66 to Kentucky on December 20, and 77-71 to Providence on January 3. AP’s bracket writeup said the committee held St. John’s nonconference résumé against it, which tells you what these results revealed: the Red Storm were excellent in league play but not flawless against top nonconference athleticism and spacing. The narrow Iowa State loss suggested they could be vulnerable when opponents match their toughness possession for possession, while Alabama’s 103 points exposed a defense that can be stressed by high-end shotmaking if it cannot fully dictate the turnover battle. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))

Pitino’s NCAA tournament history is extensive and relevant. St. John’s official prospectus states he has made 24 NCAA Tournament appearances, reached 13 Sweet 16s, 12 Elite Eights, and seven Final Fours, with national titles in 1996 at Kentucky and 2013 at Louisville. Specific years listed include Providence’s 1987 Final Four; Kentucky’s 1992 Elite Eight, 1993 Final Four, 1994 second round, 1995 Elite Eight, 1996 national title, and 1997 national runner-up finish; Louisville’s 2005 Final Four, 2007 and 2008 Elite Eights, 2009 Elite Eight, 2012 Final Four, 2013 national title, 2014 Sweet Sixteen, and 2015 Elite Eight. That résumé matters for scouting because St. John’s is not led by a coach learning March on the fly; it is led by a coach with repeated evidence of building pressure teams that travel in tournament settings. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2025/10/17/2025-26_Prospectus_FINAL.pdf))

Bottom line: St. John’s is an old-school Pitino tournament team. They win with turnover creation, offensive rebounding, frontcourt playmaking through Ejiofor, and a hard-nosed closing mentality. If an opponent protects the ball and drags them into a shotmaking contest, there is a path. But if the game gets rugged, broken, and possession-heavy, St. John’s has already shown in games against UConn, Xavier, Georgetown, Creighton, Villanova, and Seton Hall that it can bend those games to its preferred style. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_UConn_2-6_V2.pdf))
forecaster:
St. John’s enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with the profile of a team that is stronger on the résumé side than on pure offensive efficiency, and that contrast is the central fact of its statistical identity. As of games through March 15, the Red Storm were 28-6, ranked No. 16 in the NCAA NET, No. 4 in ESPN BPI, No. 10 at KenPom, and No. 15 at BartTorvik on Warren Nolan’s ranking comparison page. That mix is striking: committee-facing résumé metrics and BPI see a team closer to the national top 10, while efficiency systems are a touch cooler, especially because the offense has been good rather than dominant. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

On the possession-based side, Warren Nolan lists St. John’s with an offensive rating of 114.5 points per 100 possessions, a defensive rating of 98.2, and a net rating of +16.3. Nationally, that places them around 69th on offense, 19th on defense, and 20th in net rating. Pace is 71.0 possessions per 40 minutes, tied around 52nd nationally, so this is not an ultra-slow grinder; they play at a meaningfully above-average tempo, but the identity is still defense-first because the defensive ranking materially outpaces the offensive one. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating))

The shot-profile and possession components reinforce that picture. St. John’s has an effective field-goal percentage of 51.0%, only around 198th nationally, which is mediocre for a team with this record and seeding outlook. Their three-point attempt rate is just 0.338, around 300th nationally, so this is a notably low-volume perimeter offense in an era when many contenders lean heavily into threes. They compensate in two important ways: offensive rebounding and foul pressure. The Red Storm post a 35.9% offensive rebound rate, about 27th nationally, and a free-throw attempt rate of 0.419, about 35th nationally. In plain terms, they do not generate elite offensive value by bombing away or by hyper-efficient jump shooting; they generate it by winning the physical parts of possessions, extending trips, and getting to the line. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-efg-percent))

That is the first place where the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom. A casual observer seeing a 28-6 Big East champion might assume St. John’s is a balanced top-10 machine on both ends. The metrics say otherwise. This is a team with a top-20 defense and top-20 overall profile, but an offense that sits much closer to the national fringe of the top 70 than the top 20. The eye test may emphasize toughness, shot-making in big moments, and the aura that comes with Rick Pitino plus a 28-6 record; the data says the real engine is defensive resistance, rebounding, and free throws, not shot-quality dominance. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

Strength of schedule is solid but not overwhelming by national-contender standards. Warren Nolan’s NET strength-of-schedule page lists St. John’s at No. 62 overall and No. 38 in non-conference SOS. Earlier in the season, St. John’s own Jan. 5 game notes said the overall schedule ranked 19th nationally and the non-conference slate 27th, fifth-hardest among high majors according to KenPom at that time. The change in SOS position over the season suggests the early non-conference looked especially robust, but relative conference strength and the full-body schedule settled the profile closer to “good major-conference schedule” than “gauntlet.” ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/sos-net))

The results log shows why the résumé remains so strong. St. John’s went 18-2 in the Big East regular season, won the Big East tournament, and beat UConn twice in high-leverage spots: 81-72 on February 6 and 72-52 in the Big East title game on March 14. They also hammered Creighton 81-52 on February 21 and finished the conference tournament with wins over Providence, Seton Hall, and UConn. That closing sequence materially improved the team’s tournament profile and likely explains why résumé-oriented systems and BPI are more enthusiastic than raw offensive efficiency alone would suggest. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/sports/2025/10/8/2025-26-media-center))

Recent form, then, is clearly positive. Over their late-season run, the Red Storm looked more like a protected-seed team than a bubble-adjacent efficiency profile. While an exact last-10 adjusted efficiency split was not directly accessible from public sources in the search, the schedule/results data shows a surge built on quality wins and defensive control: wins over UConn, Providence, Marquette, Creighton, then Big East tournament wins over Providence, Seton Hall, and UConn. The 72-52 demolition of UConn in the conference final especially suggests that St. John’s entered March playing at a level above its season-long offensive baseline, or at minimum pairing decent offense with elite game-specific defense. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/sports/2025/10/8/2025-26-media-center))

So the clean analytical summary is this: St. John’s is a rugged, tournament-ready team whose statistical backbone is defense, rebounding, and free-throw generation. The offense is not aesthetically explosive by modern contender standards and, by eFG% and three-point attempt rate, it is actually fairly old-school. They do not look like the archetypal 2026 elite offense. But they do look like the kind of team that can win NCAA tournament games because they manufacture extra possessions, force opponents into lower-efficiency environments, and have proven against high-level competition that they can turn those edges into scoreboard separation. Their profile is less “unstoppable juggernaut” than “physical two-way winner with a résumé stronger than its shot-making metrics.” That gap between record and offensive efficiency is the most important thing to understand about St. John’s: the numbers do not dismiss them, but they do explain why some models see them as slightly more vulnerable than their trophy case and win total imply. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
St. John’s enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a pressure-and-possession team built around forcing mistakes, dominating the glass, living at the foul line, and turning extra possessions into paint scores rather than pure perimeter volume. Through the late-February game notes, the Red Storm were scoring 83.9 points per game, allowing 71.3, rebounding at 39.0 per game, forcing 14.3 opponent turnovers while committing only 10.8 themselves, and owning a +3.5 turnover margin. They also ranked 20th nationally in offensive rebounds per game at 13.4 and, as of Dec. 29, ranked 11th nationally in fastbreak points at 18.3 per game. Their shot profile is not isolation-heavy from three; only 565 of 1,677 field-goal attempts were threes, so 33.7% of attempts came from deep, while they averaged 731 free-throw attempts over 27 games in the February notes, an extremely high foul-drawing rate. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/28_UConn_2-25.pdf))

The style to disrupt is clear: make them play against a set floor, finish possessions with one rebound, and avoid live-ball turnovers. St. John’s is best when its defense becomes offense and when misses still become second chances. Over its 13-game winning streak cited in the UConn notes, St. John’s averaged 16.4 points off 13.5 forced turnovers, while opponents averaged only 7.5 points off 8.7 St. John’s turnovers. In that same span, the Johnnies averaged 12.4 offensive rebounds and 13.8 second-chance points, and since Jan. 6 they were averaging 6.0 more field-goal attempts and 5.2 more free-throw attempts per game than opponents. The tactical answer is therefore not abstract: you must protect the ball, keep two bodies on Zuby Ejiofor and Dillon Mitchell on the glass, and make St. John’s score over a loaded half-court shell without bailout free throws. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/28_UConn_2-25.pdf))

Named-game evidence shows what happens when opponents fail to do that. In the 92-68 win over Marquette on Jan. 13, 2026, St. John’s scored 24 points off turnovers, 48 in the paint, and 15 on second chances while leading for 39:41 of game time. In the 81-52 win over Creighton on Feb. 21, 2026, the Bluejays shot only 32.1% from the field, committed 18 turnovers, and were held to 52 points. Those are the template St. John’s wins: pressure, paint, second shots, and whistle pressure. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/27/29_Villanova_2-28.pdf))

Press vulnerability is not strongly supported by the available 2026 data; if anything, the season profile argues the opposite, because St. John’s only committed 10.8 turnovers per game on the season and just 9.1 per game during the 13-game winning streak. Providence was specifically noted in St. John’s game notes as a game in which the Johnnies committed only four turnovers on Feb. 14, 2026. Georgetown’s pregame notes also identified the Hoyas as elite at avoiding turnovers, yet St. John’s still entered that matchup on a nine-game winning streak and with strong transition production. So the evidence-based conclusion is that conventional full-court pressure is not the preferred way to attack them; ball security is too good for that to be your primary edge. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/28_UConn_2-25.pdf))

Zone is a more nuanced issue. St. John’s is not a high-volume three-point team, with only 33.7% of attempts from three, and in several wins they succeeded without bombing away. Against UConn on Feb. 6, 2026, they beat the Huskies 81-72 while shooting only 5-of-19 from three, but still won by getting to the line 31 times and winning the glass 32-26; Zuby Ejiofor posted 21 points, 10 rebounds, and seven assists, and Bryce Hopkins added 14 points with six rebounds. That suggests a compact zone can at least limit perimeter rhythm, but it only works if the zone also keeps Ejiofor off the middle and keeps Mitchell and Hopkins off offensive rebounds. Villanova provides the warning: on Jan. 17, 2026, St. John’s scored 86 on just 15 three-point attempts because Bryce Hopkins scored 20, Ian Jackson 18, Ejiofor 17, and Mitchell added 10 with 10 rebounds; the issue was interior creation and foul pressure, not jump shooting. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401822932))

Preferred pace: St. John’s wants the game fast enough for turnover conversion and fastbreak scoring, but not reckless. Their transition frequency is reflected by the 18.3 fastbreak points per game figure in late December, and game-level splits show they punish teams after mistakes. Marquette allowed 24 St. John’s points off turnovers and 10 fast-break points in the Jan. 13 loss. Xavier, even in a competitive game, saw St. John’s generate 16 points off turnovers and 14 fast-break points in an 88-83 St. John’s win on Jan. 24, 2026. To force the opposite pace, the opponent must do three specific things: use longer half-court possessions, avoid cross-court passes that fuel runouts, and send fewer bodies to the offensive glass so St. John’s cannot run off long rebounds. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2025/12/29/mens-basketball-rv-no-25-st-johns-to-close-out-2025-at-georgetown-on-wednesday))

Position-by-position matchup issues are real. At the 5, Zuby Ejiofor is the fulcrum at 6-9, 240 pounds and averaged 16.0 points, 7.1 rebounds, and 3.5 assists; he also anchored a defense that was 16th nationally in efficiency per KenPom by late February. At the 4, Dillon Mitchell is 6-8 and averaged 8.1 points, 6.9 rebounds, and 3.1 assists, giving them a switchable athlete and elite weak-side rebounder. Bryce Hopkins, listed at 6-7, 225, gives them another physical forward who can bully smaller wings and drew 10 free-throw attempts in the Villanova win. On the wing, Oziyah Sellers, Ian Jackson, and Joson Sanon are all 6-5 class guards/wings, which creates a size problem for smaller backcourts. Even off the bench, Rubén Prey and Handje Tamba are both 6-11 frontcourt options. If your 1 and 2 are small, St. John’s can post Hopkins, crash over the top with Mitchell, and switch length onto your creators. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/st-johns-ny/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Isolation versus team offense tendencies: the available public 2026 sources do not provide a trustworthy Synergy team isolation possession percentage for St. John’s, so I cannot responsibly invent one. What the available data does show is that this is more team-possession offense than pure isolation offense. They averaged 16.1 assists per game on the season with a 1.5 assist-turnover ratio, and Ejiofor’s seven-assist game against UConn is a strong example of offense running through interior touches and kickout reads rather than one player grinding every possession. Their scoring balance against Villanova also supports that: five players scored 9 or more, and four scored 10 or more. So while they have individual creators in Hopkins and Jackson, the strongest supported read is that St. John’s offense is built more on paint touches, offensive rebounding, and drive-and-kick than on ultra-high isolation share. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/28_UConn_2-25.pdf))

Coaching adaptability: Rick Pitino’s staff has strong evidence of in-game adjustment. The clearest named example in the available 2026 material is the 92-68 Marquette game, where St. John’s led 40-34 at the half and then won the second half 52-34, indicating a major post-halftime tactical edge. Villanova is another example: St. John’s led only 36-35 at halftime and then scored 50 after the break to win by seven on the road. More broadly, St. John’s improved from 10.8 turnovers per game on the season to 9.1 during the 13-game winning streak, while maintaining turnover creation and offensive rebounding. That points to a staff that sharpened strengths without sacrificing aggression. The user asked about “mid-series”; in college there are not playoff series, but within repeat-opponent settings the staff also showed adaptability by beating UConn 81-72 on Feb. 6 and then winning again in Hartford on Feb. 25, according to ESPN’s schedule/box-score listings. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/1/15/18Villanova.pdf))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must 1) cap your turnovers at single digits, because once opponents give St. John’s live-ball mistakes the game tilts toward their 18.3 fastbreak points profile; 2) gang rebound Ejiofor and Mitchell every possession, because St. John’s was at 13.4 offensive rebounds per game and turned those into 13.8 second-chance points during its winning streak; 3) wall off the paint and make their 33.7%-of-attempts-from-three offense win with jumpers over length; 4) defend without fouling, because St. John’s averaged 27.9 free-throw attempts per game as of Dec. 29 and won the UConn game despite only five made threes by generating 31 free-throw attempts; and 5) force long, patient half-court possessions instead of the turnover-and-run game that buried Marquette and Creighton. If you let St. John’s win the possession battle, they usually win the game. If you make them play one-shot half-court basketball without free throws, you have the best evidence-based path to an upset. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/news/2025/12/29/mens-basketball-rv-no-25-st-johns-to-close-out-2025-at-georgetown-on-wednesday))
